summary.text: The American Revolution was a political movement in the Thirteen Colonies of Great Britain that ran from 1765 to 1789.
It began as a colonial rebellion and grew into a revolution, and the colonies' victory in the war led to the creation of the United States.
Britain recognized American independence in the Treaty of Paris, and a more centralized federal republic followed when the Constitution took effect in 1789.

items.prompt: In 1765 colonial delegates met in New York City about new taxes passed by a Parliament in which they had no seats. What did their Declaration of Rights and Grievances argue?

options.label: That any tax was lawful if it came with a royal approval
That taxation without representation violated their rights as Englishmen
That Parliament should tax the colonies more fairly each year
That only colonial courts could judge disputes with Britain

items.explain: The delegates argued that taxing people who had no representation, among other British policies, violated their rights as Englishmen.

items.prompt: After colonists dumped taxed tea into Boston Harbor, how did Parliament respond, and what was the effect?

options.label: It repealed the taxes on tea, which calmed tensions across the colonies
It disbanded the Sons of Liberty, which ended the protests in Boston
It passed punitive laws to end self-government in Massachusetts, which increased support for revolution
It moved the colonial capital to Montreal, which split the colonies

items.explain: The Intolerable Acts were meant to end self-government in Massachusetts but instead increased American support for revolution.

items.prompt: The Second Continental Congress created an army in 1775 and needed a commander-in-chief. Who did it appoint?

options.label: George Washington
General Cornwallis
King George III
The Fox–North coalition

items.explain: Congress appointed George Washington as commander-in-chief of the Continental Army in 1775.

items.prompt: Throughout most of the war the outcome seemed uncertain. What finally pushed Britain's government to negotiate an end to its colonial rule?

options.label: The Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts that followed
Congress passing the Lee Resolution for independence
A refusal by Parliament to pay for further soldiers
A decisive victory by combined French and Continental Army forces

items.explain: Washington's combined French and American force won a decisive victory at Yorktown, which led King George III and the government to negotiate.

items.prompt: After the war the states first shared sovereignty under a looser framework. Which document later created a more centralized federal republic?

options.label: The Declaration of Rights and Grievances
The Declaration of Independence
The Constitution of the United States
The Treaty of Paris with Britain

items.explain: The states first joined under the Articles of Confederation, and a more centralized federal republic was created when the Constitution took effect in 1789.

items.prompt: On July 2, 1776, Congress passed the Lee Resolution affirming joint independence. What did it adopt unanimously two days later?

options.label: The Articles of Confederation, creating a shared sovereignty
The Declaration of Independence, arguing for separation based on inalienable rights
The Treaty of Paris, recognizing American independence
The Stamp Act Congress's list of grievances against Parliament

items.explain: On July 4, 1776, Congress unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence, arguing for separation based on inalienable rights.

paragraphs.heading: From colonies to a country
paragraphs.text: The American Revolution was a political movement in Britain's Thirteen Colonies that lasted from 1765 to 1789. It started as a rebellion by the colonies and grew into a full revolution. The colonies won the Revolutionary War, fought from 1775 to 1783, and Britain accepted their independence in the Treaty of Paris. Out of all this came a new nation, the United States.

paragraphs.heading: Roots of a separate identity
paragraphs.text: The colonies were founded in the 1600s, first under England and later under Britain after England and Scotland united in 1707. A sense of being American, rather than simply English, can be traced back to the English Civil War of 1642 to 1651. During King Philip's War, from 1675 to 1678, New England's colonies battled an alliance of a handful of Native American tribes and got no military help from England. That experience fed an identity that stood apart from being British.

paragraphs.heading: Left alone, then pressed
paragraphs.text: After England's Glorious Revolution, Britain followed a trade policy called salutary neglect, which meant leaving the colonies largely to run their own affairs. Once Britain took huge stretches of land that had belonged to New France, its leaders wanted tighter control over the colonies. The colonies, in turn, wanted their old freedom to govern themselves back. Discontent began soon after the French and Indian War ended in 1763.

paragraphs.heading: Taxes and protest
paragraphs.text: Parliament placed new taxes on the colonists, officially to cover the costs of the war, even though the colonies had fought in it and backed it. In 1765, delegates from several colonies met in New York City at the Stamp Act Congress. Their Declaration of Rights and Grievances argued that being taxed without a voice in Parliament broke their rights as Englishmen. The Stamp Act was later repealed, but the Townshend Acts raised tensions again.

paragraphs.heading: Boston at the center
paragraphs.text: King George III sent troops to Massachusetts to calm the growing rebellion, and this led to the Boston Massacre in 1770. In December 1773, members of the Sons of Liberty threw chests of taxed tea belonging to the British East India Company into Boston Harbor, an act called the Boston Tea Party. Parliament struck back with harsh laws known as the Intolerable Acts, meant to end self-government in Massachusetts. Instead, those laws won the revolution more support.

paragraphs.heading: War and independence
paragraphs.text: British efforts to disarm the colonists led to the Battles of Lexington and Concord, which started the war. The Second Continental Congress, which acted as a temporary government, created the Continental Army in 1775 and named George Washington its commander. On July 2, 1776, Congress passed the Lee Resolution in favor of independence. Two days later it unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence, which grounded the break on rights that cannot be taken away.

paragraphs.heading: Yorktown and the peace
paragraphs.text: For most of the war, nobody could be sure who would win, and France and Spain eventually joined in. In 1781, French and Continental forces under Washington took General Cornwallis's British army prisoner at the Siege of Yorktown. After that defeat, Parliament moved toward ending the war on American terms. In the Treaty of Paris of 1783, Britain recognized the United States and handed over almost all the land below the Great Lakes and east of the Mississippi River.

paragraphs.heading: A new kind of government
paragraphs.text: During the war, the states shared their sovereignty under the Articles of Confederation. Later the Constitution, which took effect in 1789, created a more centralized federal republic, and the Bill of Rights followed in 1791. The United States became the first nation to set up a federal republic with a written constitution resting on natural rights, on government by the people's consent, and on equal treatment by the law. Its democracy was still limited, though, compared with how the idea developed later.
